871.quote_or_event: “Everything that happens to somebody, affects him personally; therefore, knowing the creatures' love of their own self, do not deprive them of their life, but cease from endangering and combating them.”
871.explanation: Because every being cherishes its own life, Mahāvīra's teaching forbids not only killing but all hostility toward other creatures. The daily Jain confession (pratikramaṇa) says the same in its well-known formula: friendship toward all beings and enmity toward none.
871.tie_back: The Kural calls enmity a thing with no goodness in it, not to be wanted even in jest, and the Jain teaching rules out enmity toward any creature in any form at all.
871.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 6.6 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com); cf. the Prakrit kṣamāpanā verse ‘khāmemi savve jīvā’ of the Āvaśyaka/pratikramaṇa liturgy
871._accuracy_note: Only the Uttarādhyayana verse is quoted, checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. The kṣamāpanā formula is paraphrased because no stable scholarly English rendering could be verified in this session. Neither text has the Kural's 'even in jest'.

872.quote_or_event: “You may as well dig rocks with your nails, or eat iron with your teeth, or kick fire with your feet, as treat contemptuously a monk.”
872.explanation: When the priests' young men beat the sage Harikeśa, Bhadrā warns them that to make an enemy of a holy man of disciplined mind is like attacking rock, iron and fire: only the attacker is hurt.
872.tie_back: The Kural warns never to make enemies of those whose plough is the word, and Bhadrā's warning likewise makes the wise sage the one opponent it is ruinous to provoke.
872.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 12.26 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
872._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. A strong fit for 'do not make enemies of the wise', though Harikeśa's power lies in ascetic virtue rather than in eloquence, and the Kural's contrast with warriors is missing.

873.quote_or_event: “A cruel man does cruel acts and is thereby involved in other cruelties; but sinful undertakings will in the end bring about misery.”
873.explanation: Jacobi's note glosses the 'cruel man' (veri) as vairin, literally 'one who bears enmity'. The verse says such a man becomes caught in ever-widening hostility that ends in his own misery.
873.tie_back: The Kural calls the lone man who makes many enemies worse than a madman, and the Jain verse shows how the man of enmity piles up further hostilities until they ruin him.
873.source: Sūtrakṛtāṅga I.8.7, with Jacobi's note (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; wisdomlib.org)
873._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on wisdomlib.org, including the note 'Veri = vairin'. Lacks the Kural's key images of standing alone and of folly worse than madness, so it is a next-best match.

874.quote_or_event: “There is not the least hatred in me, neither now, nor before, nor in future. …” ‘You know the truth and the Law; you are not angry, compassionate sage; we take refuge at your feet, we together with all of them.’
874.explanation: After the priests and their followers have beaten him, the sage Harikeśa declares that he has no hatred at all, and his former attackers become his devotees and take refuge with him.
874.tie_back: The Kural praises the noble person who turns enemies into friends, and Harikeśa, holding no enmity, turns his attackers into people who seek refuge at his feet.
874.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 12.32–33 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
874._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com; the rest of 12.32 is cut at the ellipsis. The change of heart is helped by the Yakṣas' punishment of the attackers, not by the sage's goodness alone, so the fit is good but partial.

875.quote_or_event: “Knowing the thoughts of their pupils, both Keśi and Gautama made up their minds to meet each other. Gautama, knowing what is proper and what is due to the older section (of the church), went to the Tinduka park, accompanied by the crowd, his pupils. When Keśi, the young monk, saw Gautama approach, he received him with all becoming attention.”
875.explanation: The followers of Pārśva and of Mahāvīra were uneasy about their differences, so the two leaders met and turned a possible rivalry into union, and Keśi in the end adopted Mahāvīra's five vows.
875.tie_back: The Kural advises a man facing two adversaries to make one of them a friendly ally, and Gautama's courteous approach to Keśi turns a potential rival community into an ally.
875.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 23.14–16 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; wisdomlib.org)
875._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on wisdomlib.org. Keśi and Gautama were never enemies, and there is no second adversary or strategic motive, so this is only a next-best parallel of rivalry turned into alliance.

876.quote_or_event: “Benevolence (maitrī) towards all living-beings (sattva), joy (pramoda) at the sight of the virtuous (guṇādhika), compassion and sympathy (kāruṇya) for the afflicted (kliśyamāna), and tolerance (mādhyasthya) towards the insolent and ill-behaved (avineya) are the other observances.”
876.explanation: Umāsvāti's sūtra prescribes mādhyasthya, a neutral stance toward the insolent. Pūjyapāda's commentary defines it as freedom from both attachment and revulsion.
876.tie_back: The Kural advises keeping a careful middle distance in a crisis, neither committing to a doubtful person nor breaking with him, and Jain mādhyasthya is a stance of neither embrace nor rejection.
876.source: Tattvārtha Sūtra 7.11, with Pūjyapāda's Sarvārthasiddhi (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018; wisdomlib.org)
876._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Vijay K. Jain's translation on wisdomlib.org. Mādhyasthya is a spiritual attitude rather than a tactic for times of crisis, but its 'neither attachment nor revulsion' corresponds well to the Kural's neither trusting nor breaking.

877.quote_or_event: “If he suffers from the heat of hot things, or from the heat of his body, or from the heat of summer, he should not lament the loss of comfort. … All these troubles have been declared by the Kāśyapa. A monk should not be vanquished by them, when attacked by any anywhere.”
877.explanation: Mahāvīra's teaching on the twenty-two hardships (parīṣaha) asks the monk to bear them without complaint and never to let them defeat him.
877.tie_back: The Kural says not to pour out one's troubles or show weakness before enemies, and the Jain discipline likewise forbids lamenting one's sufferings and calls for firmness against every attack.
877.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 2.8 and closing passage (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; wisdomlib.org)
877._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on wisdomlib.org. The 'attackers' here are hardships rather than human enemies, and the Kural's point about whom one confides in is not addressed, so the match is partial.

878.quote_or_event: “Making Faith his fortress, Penance and Self-control the bolt (of its gate), Patience its strong wall, so that guarded in three ways it is impregnable; making Zeal his bow, its string Carefulness in walking (iriyâ), and its top (where the string is fastened) Content, he should bend (this bow) with Truth, piercing with the arrow, Penance, (the foe's) mail, Karman--(in this way) a sage will be the victor in battle and get rid of the Samsâra.”
878.explanation: Asked by Indra to fortify his city, King Nami describes instead an inner fortress and an inner bow, built from the virtues, with which the sage defeats karma.
878.tie_back: The Kural says to know the method, build up your strength and guard yourself so that the enemy's pride withers, and Nami's fortress-and-bow image gives the same three steps in Jain form, aimed against karma.
878.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 9.20–22 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
878._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com (Jacobi's Saṃsâra is written here as Samsâra). A strong structural parallel of defence plus strength leading to victory, though the enemy is karma rather than a human rival.

879.quote_or_event: ‘O Gautama, in the innermost heart there grows a plant which brings forth poisonous fruit; how have you torn it out?’ “I have thoroughly clipped that plant, and torn it out altogether with its roots; thus I have got rid of the poisonous fruit.” … “Love of existence is that dreadful plant which brings forth dreadful fruit; having regularly torn it out, I live pleasantly.”
879.explanation: In the dialogue between Keśi and Gautama, craving for existence is pictured as a poisonous plant growing in the heart, which the sage must pull out by the roots.
879.tie_back: The Kural tells us to cut down the thorn tree while it is young, before it can wound the hand, and Gautama likewise speaks of uprooting a harmful growth completely before it bears its poisonous fruit.
879.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 23.45–46, 48 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; wisdomlib.org)
879._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on wisdomlib.org. The plant-uprooting image is a close match, but the Kural's point about timing (act while it is young) is not explicit, and the 'enemy' is inner craving.

880.quote_or_event: ‘Gautama, you stand in the midst of many thousand (foes) who make an attack on you; how have you vanquished them?’ “By vanquishing one, five are vanquished; by vanquishing five, ten are vanquished; by this tenfold victory, I vanquish all foes.”
880.explanation: Gautama goes on to explain that these foes are the unconquered self, the four passions (anger, pride, deceit and greed) and the five senses, and that crushing them is the only victory that counts.
880.tie_back: The Kural says those who cannot break the pride of hostile foes do not truly live, and the Jain sage claims a complete victory over every foe, pride among them, by conquering them within.
880.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 23.35–36 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; wisdomlib.org)
880._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on wisdomlib.org. The Jain text turns the Kural's outer enemies into inner passions, so the match is real only through that reinterpretation.
